real_qa.r: Epirus combines high-powered and high-energy microwave capabilities using gallium nitride semiconductors, allowing the system to stay active inside target electronics for extended periods rather than nanoseconds. The system uses an arbitrary waveform software-defined approach implemented through phased arrays that can scan a 60-by-60 degree section of sky in less than a second, creating a persistent temporal field. Additionally, gallium nitride semiconductors can withstand enormous energies and heat fluxes—higher heat flux than on the surface of the sun—and have doubled in power density every few years.

real_qa.q: How does Epirus's software-defined system maintain effectiveness against evolving counter-drone defenses without requiring hardware changes?
real_qa.r: The system can be reprogrammed to counter new drone defenses in minutes or days without changing hardware. Epirus operates the software as a cat-and-mouse game where when adversaries modify shielding or electronics, the company's software tools—including polarization selection, frequency variation, pulse changes, and pulse repetition rates—can be adapted quickly. This forces adversaries back into expensive military-grade hardware modifications rather than simple software-based countermeasures.

real_qa.q: Why does counter-drone technology based on signal jamming become ineffective against autonomous drone swarms, and what approach does Epirus take instead?
real_qa.r: Advances in AI and autonomous navigation have eliminated the dependency on external signals for drone control, making traditional signal jamming impossible as drones now operate independently without any connectivity to the outside world.
